answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Spoken by Henry Tilney in Chapter 14 of Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey, written by 1799 and published posthumously in December 1817 (title page dated 1818). The exact wording is confirmed in the original text.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: “But you never read novels, I dare say?” — “Why not?” — “Because they are not clever enough for you—gentlemen read better books.” — “The person, be it gentleman or lady, who has not pleasure in a good novel, must be intolerably stupid. I have read all Mrs. Radcliffe's works, and most of them with great pleasure.”
trail: Written by Jane Austen and completed by about 1799, decades before publication (Wikipedia ↗).
Published posthumously by John Murray in December 1817 alongside Persuasion, with the title page dated 1818 (Wikipedia ↗).
The exact wording appears verbatim in Chapter 14, spoken by Henry Tilney (Wikisource, Northanger Abbey, Chapter 14 ↗).
Freely available in the public-domain Project Gutenberg edition of the novel (Project Gutenberg ↗).
source.excerptNote: Henry Tilney's reply after Catherine assumes he wouldn't stoop to novel-reading.
source.rightsNote: Northanger Abbey was first published in December 1817, well over a century before the 1931 cutoff, so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Jane Austen
author.heading: About Jane Austen
author.bio: Jane Austen wrote six major novels — including Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility, and Northanger Abbey — that combine social comedy with sharp moral observation. Northanger Abbey, her wry send-up of Gothic fiction and its critics, was completed by 1799 but not published until after her death in 1817.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This line is genuinely Austen's own writing and is correctly credited to her. The one nuance worth flagging is who, within the story, actually says it.

items.why: Often print the line as a flat Jane Austen maxim without noting it is dialogue spoken by the character Henry Tilney, not narration or a statement in Austen's own voice.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Austen's, written for Henry Tilney in Chapter 14 of Northanger Abbey ↗ — confirmed verbatim in the original text, just delivered by a character rather than the narrator.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Henry Tilney says this to Catherine Morland after she assumes he doesn't read novels because “gentlemen read better books.” He answers that anyone — man or woman — who takes no pleasure in a good novel “must be intolerably stupid,” then confesses he devoured Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho in two days flat, unable to put it down.

The line sits inside Austen's broader defence of novel-reading in Northanger Abbey, a genre then widely dismissed — including by novelists themselves — as frivolous, especially for women. It is dialogue given to a witty, sympathetic character, not a narrator's aside, but it reads as Austen's own case for the novel as a serious form.
detailsBody: Catherine's assumption — that gentlemen don't read novels — reflects a real prejudice of the period; Austen has Henry puncture it directly, and elsewhere in the same novel steps outside the story to mount an explicit authorial defence of novels as a form (the famous “only a novel...” passage in Chapter 5).
